problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$

examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x \,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \, \rm{m/s}^2.$ If $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x = 1 \, \textrm m.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/4fdd70a4ca80965c0adce9c60be36b0712852b662cff69f9733f50c739fd1b32.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

feedback.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{1}{x+1}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/473a3f91d91351499d5849ee07a86cfcfc2b257949d6ebba68b3261201f2bf68.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{1}{x+1}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{x+1}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{x+1}.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{x+1}.
$$
